<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values across all 20 models (ranging from -24.11 to -23.71). This indicates that a standard baseline condition is insufficient to distinguish the mechanisms, as all models possess enough flexibility to fit a simple kinetic curve by adjusting their rate constants.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but the results confirm the necessity of strongly perturbing the system to break the degeneracy between the models.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To effectively separate the models, we need to probe their non-linear dependencies on catalyst, substrate, and product concentrations simultaneously. 
1. By setting the initial product concentration to its maximum (P = 0.5), we will strongly differentiate models that feature product-induced deactivation or product-involved catalysis (e.g., M5, M12, M17) from those that do not.
2. By increasing the catalyst concentration to its maximum (cat = 0.20), we will amplify the effects of higher-order catalyst interactions, such as dimerization or bimolecular deactivation (e.g., M2, M3, M13, M18, M19). These models will scale non-linearly compared to first-order catalyst models.
3. By increasing the substrate concentration (S = 2.0), we will further test substrate-dependent deactivation or higher-order substrate binding (e.g., M7, M11, M16).
This combined perturbation will force the models to extrapolate far from the baseline condition, leading to a significant divergence in their fitting capabilities and reducing uncertainty across the entire set of mechanisms.
</hypothesis>
